extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political economy, education policy, and philosophy; policymakers and general educated public
extracted.subtask_description: Principled criteria and observations for judging and designing curricula, pedagogy, institutional organization, and the public role in education (historical and normative). Emphasizes what should be taught, in what order, who it should serve, and how teachers and institutions ought to be incentivized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach logic before advanced subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The student ought to understand well the difference between good and bad reasoning before he was led to reason upon subjects of so great importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Logic (the science of the general principles of good and bad reasoning) should be taught prior to physics and ethics because examining conflicting philosophical systems leads to distinguishing probable from demonstrative arguments and fallacious from conclusive ones. This prepares students to judge other sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experiment and observation over metaphysical subtleties
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper subject of experiment and observation ... was almost entirely neglected. The subject ... in which the most careful attention can discover nothing but obscurity and uncertainty ... was greatly cultivated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curricula should focus on sciences amenable to experiment (physics) rather than on metaphysics/pneumatics/ontology composed largely of subtleties and sophisms. Over-emphasis on speculative metaphysics is an anti-pattern that yields little useful discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral philosophy should promote present-life happiness and practical virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherein consisted the happiness and perfection of a man ... was the object which the ancient moral philosophy proposed to investigate. In the modern philosophy, it was frequently represented as ... inconsistent with any degree of happiness in this life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral instruction should aim at improving conduct and heart in this life (liberal, generous, and spirited conduct), not primarily at ascetic penance for a life to come. Casuistry and ascetic morality are criticized as corrupting moral philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making curricula merely subservient to theology
rubrics_metrics.description: In the universities of Europe, where philosophy was taught only as subservient to theology, it was natural to dwell longer upon these two chapters than upon any other of the science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When universities teach primarily to serve theological ends, they tend to expand obscure disciplines (pneumatology, doctrine of spirits) at the expense of useful experimental sciences. Educational institutions should not be narrowly tailored only to prepare ecclesiastics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions should be responsive to intellectual improvements and public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The improvements which, in modern times have been made in several different branches of philosophy, have not, the greater part of them, been made in universities ... the richest and best endowed universities have been slowest in adopting those improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Universities and learned societies should adapt to genuine intellectual advances; endowments and institutional privileges can produce institutional inertia and resistance to change. Poorer schools tied to reputation/fees may adopt improvements faster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design teacher remuneration and privileges to preserve accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The endowments of schools and colleges have in this manner not only corrupted the diligence of public teachers ... The private teacher ... is, in modern times, generally considered as in the very lowest order of men of letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When public salaries or institutional privileges make teachers independent of their reputation, diligence suffers. Conversely, private teachers reliant on reputation can be more attentive, but unequal institutional privileges make competition unfair and discourage good private instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary education (reading, writing, arithmetic) is essential and public responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The most essential parts of education, however, to read, write, and account, can be acquired at so early a period of life ... For a very small expense, the public can facilitate, can encourage and can even impose upon almost the whole body of the people, the necessity of acquiring those most essential parts of education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State should facilitate basic schooling by establishing local (parish/district) schools where children can be taught at moderate cost; the master should be partly but not wholly paid by the public to maintain accountability. Examples: Scottish parish schools, English charity schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public attention especially needed for education of the labouring poor
rubrics_metrics.description: In the progress of the division of labour ... the understandings of the greater part of men are necessarily formed by their ordinary employments ... This torpor of his mind renders him ... incapable of conceiving any generous, noble, or tender sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the division of labour in civilized, commercial societies tends to deaden the intellect and civic virtues of the labouring poor, the state must take pains (e.g., provide elementary education) to prevent widespread degeneracy and preserve basic capacities for citizenship and defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid early unstructured travel as a substitute for education
rubrics_metrics.description: In England, it becomes every day more and more the custom to send young people to travel in foreign countries immediately upon their leaving school ... He generally returns home more conceited, more unprincipled, more dissipated ... and more incapable of any serious application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sending adolescents abroad too early often wastes formative years and undermines habits of study and seriousness; travel at a very young age is an anti-pattern compared to more structured education or later travel after maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women's education should be practical, targeted to social roles
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no public institutions for the education of women, and there is accordingly nothing useless, absurd, or fantastical, in the common course of their education. ... Every part of their education tends evidently to some useful purpose ... to form their mind to reserve, to modesty, to chastity, and to economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education for women is defended as being narrowly practical and useful (domestic management, personal attractions, proper behaviour). The point is normative: teach what parents/guardians judge necessary for their social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical training (gymnastics) serves civic/military ends; cultural arts have contested moral effects
rubrics_metrics.description: By gymnastic exercises, it was intended to harden his body, to sharpen his courage, and to prepare him for the fatigues and dangers of war. ... By the other part, music, it was proposed ... to humanize the mind, to soften the temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical education is clearly instrumental for martial readiness and civic robustness; inclusion of music/arts is justified as humanizing but its actual effect on public morals is questioned by comparison of Greek and Roman history (music may not have improved Greek morals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional design (courts, precedents) shapes public character and legal system
rubrics_metrics.description: At Rome, the principal courts ... consisted either of a single judge, or of a small number of judges ... This attention to practice and precedent, necessarily formed the Roman law into that regular and orderly system ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The structure of public institutions (e.g., smaller, responsible courts versus large mobbish assemblies) affects civic character, respect for oaths, and the development of systematic law—an indirectly relevant criterion when evaluating the broader educational and civic effects of institutions.
